samples.summary: 'settles after one heal and stays on the healed slide' is vacuous — it cannot fail even if the heal re-runs every frame
samples.evidence: The test sets up 2 slides, makes slideIds[1] current (index 1) and removes it, then asserts after 3 frames that the cursor is slideIds[0]. `resolveCurrentSlide` computes `nextIdx = Math.min(Math.max(this.currentIndex - 1, 0), len - 1)` (editor.ts:1534) which floors at 0, and after the heal the deck holds exactly one slide. So even a hypothetically broken implementation that healed on every frame and walked the cursor backwards each time would still land on slideIds[0] — the stated claim ('repeated frames must not keep walking the cursor backwards') is untestable in this configuration. It would need e.g. 3+ slides with the cursor healed to a non-zero index (start at index 2, remove it, assert it stays at index 1 over repeated frames).

finding.summary: 'settles after one heal and stays on the healed slide' is vacuous — it cannot fail even if the heal re-runs every frame
finding.evidence: The test sets up 2 slides, makes slideIds[1] current (index 1) and removes it, then asserts after 3 frames that the cursor is slideIds[0]. `resolveCurrentSlide` computes `nextIdx = Math.min(Math.max(this.currentIndex - 1, 0), len - 1)` (editor.ts:1534) which floors at 0, and after the heal the deck holds exactly one slide. So even a hypothetically broken implementation that healed on every frame and walked the cursor backwards each time would still land on slideIds[0] — the stated claim ('repeated frames must not keep walking the cursor backwards') is untestable in this configuration. verdict.reason: Verified the test and the implementation. The test uses setup(2) with the cursor on slideIds[1] (index 1) and removes that slide, leaving a single-slide deck; resolveCurrentSlide's nextIdx = Math.min(Math.max(currentIndex-1,0), len-1) is therefore pinned to 0 (editor.ts:1534-1537). So the assertion `getCurrentSlideId() === slideIds[0]` after 3 frames holds even for an implementation that re-heals every frame and decrements the index each time — the stated claim ("Repeated frames must not keep walking the cursor backwards", test line 222) is not exercised. The only thing the assertion can detect (that a heal happened at all) is already covered by the tests at lines 167-178 and 192-213, and the nested-resolve test at 227-250 is also a 2-slide/index-1 setup so it cannot distinguish either. A discriminating case needs >=3 slides with the heal landing on a non-zero index. Real fake-coverage for the advertised behavior; in-lane and major under the test-adequacy rubric.

finding.summary: Crop/text-edit teardown tests can't distinguish 'discard' from 'commit'
finding.evidence: `resolveCurrentSlide` deliberately calls `exitImageCrop(false)` and `exitEditMode('cancel')` (editor.ts:1550-1551), and both the source comment and the test comment ("so it is discarded rather than committed — a commit would write to nowhere", test:267-268) present that as the behavior under test. But the assertions are only `expect(ed.isCropping()).toBe(false)` (test:272) and `expect(ed.isTextEditing()).toBe(false)` (test:248) — both hold identically if the code were changed to `exitImageCrop(true)` / `exitEditMode('commit')`, since commit also exits the session. Nothing asserts the store was not mutated (e.g. comparing the element's crop rect / blocks in `store.read()` before and after, or that no extra undo entry was pushed), so the discard-vs-commit choice ships untested.

verdict.reason:
The finding's central claim — that `expect(ed.isCropping()).toBe(false)` "hold[s] identically if the code were changed to `exitImageCrop(true)`" — is verifiably false, and the crop test is itself the counterexample.

Trace of the hypothetical mutation: in the crop test the image and its slide are both removed (current-slide-heal.test.ts:257-269), and `cropSession.slideId` is the removed slide id (editor.ts:2401-2411). If `resolveCurrentSlide` called `exitImageCrop(true)` instead of `(false)`, `exitImageCrop` would run `commitCropFrame` (editor.ts:2449-2458), which unconditionally does `store.batch(() => store.updateElementFrame(session.slideId, …))` (editor.ts:2503-2511). `MemSlidesStore.updateElementFrame` calls `requireSlide`, which throws `Slide not found: …` (memory.ts:694-695, 1828-1831), and `batch()` does not swallow — `fn()` is wrapped only in `try/finally` (memory.ts:1789-1803). `exitImageCrop` likewise only has `finally { finishCropSession() }` and no `catch` (editor.ts:2448-2461), so the error propagates out of `resolveCurrentSlide` → `render()` (editor.ts:1388-1389, 1426-1427; no try/catch anywhere in that path) → the test's `frame(ed)` helper (test:96-99, called at test:270). The test would go RED before reaching line 272. So the discard-vs-commit choice for the crop path is latched by the existing test, contrary to the finding.

The text half of the finding is real but minor, not blocking under this lens: `exitEditMode('commit')` routes through the text box's `onCommit`, whose store write is deliberately wrapped in `try { … } catch { /* element may have been removed */ }` (editor.ts:4117-4165), so a commit on a removed slide makes no observable document change at all. The only residual difference is one dead snapshot pushed onto `MemSlidesStore.undoStack` before the swallowed throw (memory.ts:1789-1793) — i.e. "coverage could be broader" (a `store.canUndo()`-depth assertion), while the core teardown behavior (session torn down, cursor healed, selection dropped) is genuinely asserted and would fail if the teardown regressed (test:240-249, 265-273). That is a minor breadth gap, not a vacuous test or an untested behavior change.
